title: Stanford's Fingernail-Sized Chip Untangles Mixed Light Into Clean Beams
excerpt: A silicon photonic chip has, for the first time, taken partially coherent light from multiple lasers and sorted it into separate, pure beams — work published in Nature Photonics that could sharpen microscopy and astronomy.
body:
• Stanford engineers and colleagues built a photonic chip the size of a fingernail that takes in mixed, partially coherent light and outputs separated, pure beams — a first demonstration, published October 30 in Nature Photonics.
  • In tests the chip sorted light from two infrared lasers, then three, and separated the two strongest coherence modes with more than 98% fidelity against a reference method.
  • The team is collaborating with NASA on whether the approach could help analyse light from distant galaxies; microscopy, sensing and communications are the other named uses.
  • For readers: this is laboratory work, not a product — its significance is that a separation theorised since the 1980s now exists in hardware.

Most light that reaches a camera is a muddle. Photons from different sources overlap, their oscillations lining up only briefly before falling out of step, and conventional imaging records the mixture rather than the ingredients. A team led by Stanford engineers has built a chip that unmixes it. According to Stanford's report of the work, it is the first time researchers have demonstrated a device that can take in mixed, or partially coherent, light and sort its photons into a clear set of separate beams.

How the chip works

The device is a silicon photonic circuit — a chip that channels photons for processing the way an electronic chip channels electrons — containing a network of interferometers. A self-configuring algorithm tunes that network to identify the dominant coherence modes in the incoming light and physically route them to separate outputs. The chip does not simply recover the original laser sources; it diagonalises the light field's coherency matrix, separating the field into components that are mutually incoherent — statistically independent of each other. The same architecture can also run in reverse, the researchers said, to generate partially coherent light with a chosen structure.

What the tests showed

The team pointed two infrared lasers into the chip, mixing the sources into partially coherent light, and the chip sorted the mixture automatically by source. They then directed the separated beams through a device that mixed them again: the beams would not sync up, demonstrating they were genuinely independent. Adding a third laser, the chip still sorted the mixture into pure beams. Interesting Engineering's account adds the measurement detail: using a nine-input device, the team separated the two strongest coherence modes with more than 98% fidelity against a reference tomography method, and verified the approach beyond two modes in a separate three-mode experiment. The paper, by Paul-Alexis Mor and colleagues, appeared in Nature Photonics (DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-02035-6).

"Our chip learns the underlying coherence modes of an unknown light field and physically directs them into separate outputs."

— Shanhui Fan, Professor of Electrical Engineering, Stanford

Why it matters, and what is next

Separating overlapping light sources can recover depth and source information that standard cameras miss, which is why the named applications are microscopy, astronomy, sensing and optical communication. Stanford professors David Miller and Olav Solgaard, PhD student Annie Kroo and colleagues are now collaborating with NASA to see whether the technology could probe light from distant galaxies. Scaling the approach to larger numbers of optical modes remains the open engineering problem — the demonstration handles a handful of modes, and real-world scenes carry far more.
